plan.topic: Skin feels sore, tingly or sensitive to touch on a GLP-1 medicine (dysesthesia): what's reported, how uncommon it is, and when to tell your prescriber
plan.angle: Semaglutide (Wegovy): skin sore, tingly or sensitive to touch? It's a known, labeled effect, and it's more common at the higher dose. Give the label's per-arm rates for dysesthesia and related skin-sensation events: 7.2 mg vs 2.4 mg vs placebo, in adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition, quoted exactly from the live Wegovy PI. Say the cause isn't known. Untagged line: tell your prescriber, especially if it spreads or gets worse. Then the full Medication Guide allergy emergency card with 'right away', the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. Don't mention tirzepatide, and don't use 'uncommon'. New working title: 'Semaglutide (Wegovy): Skin Sore or Tingly to Touch? #shorts'.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Skin Sore or Tingly to Touch? #shorts
plan.why: A felt symptom with almost no creator coverage, in the calm 'Is this normal?' format that wins for us. It is early on a rising signal and comes with an evidence-first caution angle. | fact-check: The evidence is about semaglutide, not tirzepatide. Dysesthesia and related altered skin sensations are characterized for semaglutide in the STEP UP trials and the Wegovy labeling. For 7.2 mg (Wegovy HD, FDA-approved 19 Mar 2026), reported rates are about 22–23% vs about 6% on 2.4 mg and 0% on placebo, and STEP UP T2D gave 18.9% / 4.9% / 0%. Tirzepatide has only case reports and FAERS signals, and it isn't listed on the Zepbound or Mounjaro label. The working title 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro)' would therefore misattribute the data, so it has to change. The proposed relief line 'It's reported, and uncommon' is FALSE at 7.2 mg, where it's roughly 1 in 5. 'Uncommon' can't be used. Base the figures on the live Wegovy PI table, not news or Noom or Ro blogs, and give the population (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition) and the comparator. Name the grouped terms only as the label lists them. Say the cause isn't known. Mention the Medsafe NZ March 2026 article as context only if it's needed. Leave out case reports, creams and supplements.

package.description:
Sore, tingly or sensitive skin on semaglutide (Wegovy) is named in the label: dysesthesia, not "in your head." About 1 in 5 on 7.2 mg, about 6 in 100 on 2.4 mg, essentially none on placebo (adults with obesity, 72 weeks). Tell your prescriber, especially if it spreads or gets worse.
Serious allergy signs need emergency help right away: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching; fainting or feeling dizzy; very rapid heartbeat. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
#Semaglutide
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

The spoken close is "Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber." followed by the loop line "So next time:", which runs back into sentence 1. Post note for Exp G: set the related-video link to the Side Effects long video. It's the closest match, since there's no skin long video. Fact-check REVISE fixes from 11-22, applied word for word: (1) s3 stat_label now reads placebo 0.3% (US label), "7.2 mg injection" and "adults with obesity with or without type 2 diabetes". (2) s4 items now show "Placebo: 0.3% (about 3 in 1,000)" and "Adults with obesity (BMI 30+), with or without type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks". (3) The s2 fact now reads "more often on 7.2 mg than on 2.4 mg". (4) s3 on_screen_text now says "Wegovy 7.2 mg injection: dysesthesia in about 1 in 5". The spoken "essentially none" stays, since the fact-checker cleared it (0.3% is about 3 in 1,000). The allergy and don't-stop lines are untagged house safety lines. Check on the TTS transcript: "dysesthesia", "seven point two milligrams", "two point four milligrams" and "seventy-two weeks". Note for the Motion Designer: build captions from the on_screen_text field using digits ("7.2 MG", "0.3%", "1 IN 5"). factcheck.summary:
I checked every claim against the current Wegovy Prescribing Information on DailyMed (revised June 18, 2026). Everything holds up.

- **Dose and rates:** the label includes the 7.2 mg (Wegovy HD) injection. Table 4 lists dysesthesia at 22% on 7.2 mg, 6% on 2.4 mg and 0.3% on placebo, over 72 weeks.
- **Population:** Studies 8 and 9 enrolled adults with obesity (BMI ≥30), with and without type 2 diabetes.
- **Related events:** the dysesthesia subsection names paresthesia, pain of skin, sensitive skin and burning skin sensation. That matches "sore, tingly skin" and the s3 stat label.
- **"Doesn't explain why":** the label gives no mechanism, so s5 is accurate.

**Rounding and framing**
- 22% as "about 1 in 5", 6% as "about 6 in 100" and 0.3% as "essentially none / about 3 in 1,000" are all fair.
- Every number names its dose and comparator, and the spoken population and timeframe are present.
- The "all in your head" hook is a rhetorical myth-flip that is corrected straight away, not a false claim.

**Safety lines**
- The allergy list follows the house Medication Guide wording in full and keeps "right away".
- The don't-stop line is scoped correctly, and the "Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber." card is one whole card ending in a full stop.
- There's no dosing, switching or stopping advice.

**Word count:** I count about 116 spoken words, inside the tight arm.

**Not changed, on purpose:** the spoken s4 line says only "adults with obesity", without "with or without type 2 diabetes". That's narrower, not wrong, and the on-screen list carries the full population. Adding six words would push the script past 120, so I'm not flagging it.

**Optional:** the label also says most people whose 7.2 mg dose was stopped, paused or lowered recovered from the event. That's verified if you want it in a future long video; this Short doesn't need it.

On the SFX side the main issue was redundancy: many cue pairs/triples (pop+whip, swell+whoosh, pop+tick, swoosh+swoosh+tick+pop) fired within the same 0.1-0.4s window — I dropped the duplicate layer in each cluster and kept the most characterful one (keeping transition-matched sounds like whip/swoosh where relevant). A handful of cues that were too hot during speech (around -12 dB, e.g. i4-i6, i14, i21, i24) were pulled down toward the -14 to -20 dB speech-SFX window, and one pause-only cue cluster (i31/i32) that had sunk to -18 dB was brought back up toward the -8 to -10 dB pause/transition target. Added three safe, non-medical custom accents (a soft shimmer for the stat reveal, a warm chime for the reassurance beat, and a gentle room-tone bed at the open) — nothing imitates injecting, needles, pens or pills, per the medical-safety rule.
